answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and zero buffer, any supplier disruption risk is unacceptable right now, ruling out switching primary vendor or adding a second source this cycle despite c2's cost-cutting appeal—that memory reflects a single onboarding cycle and doesn't address sustained delivery reliability under tight capacity. The contract's imminent 14-day expiration also forecloses deferring the decision (c5 applied to a non-critical service, not one expiring under volume pressure). Renewing outright without renegotiation leaves the 18% mandate unaddressed. Negotiating terms at renewal (c4) combined with the incumbent's demonstrated multi-year volume pricing leverage (c6) and proven integration stability (c1) offers the best path to cut cost without touching the qualified, reliable supply chain. I verified c4 and c2 specifically because they carry the most weight for and against a vendor switch versus negotiation, and I want the original context on how much margin recovery and how durable the vendor-switch savings actually were before locking in a direction.
